title: 01. Fundamentals & Trade-offs: SLA, SLO, SLI

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** An **SLI** is the measured indicator of service health (e.g., "99.95% of requests returned in < 100 ms"), an **SLO** is the target you set for that indicator (e.g., "99.9% availability over 28 days"), and an **SLA** is the contractual consequence of missing the target (e.g., "99.9% or we refund 10% of your bill").

SLI, SLO, and SLA form a hierarchy that turns fuzzy reliability goals into engineering decisions. The **SLI** (Service Level Indicator) is a measurement — a number that comes out of your telemetry. The **SLO** (Service Level Objective) is the target value you commit to internally — what "good enough" looks like for users. The **SLA** (Service Level Agreement) is the legal/business contract with customers — what happens if you miss. Google's SRE book formalized this hierarchy, and the principle is simple: *measure (SLI) → target (SLO) → contract (SLA)*. Crucially, the SLA is always *looser* than the SLO, which is always *looser* than the actual observed reliability — you build in a safety margin so that a bad week doesn't trigger customer refunds.

Consider **AWS S3**. Its SLA promises 99.9% monthly availability; if AWS breaches, customers get a 10% service credit. Internally, AWS's SLO for S3 is much stricter — closer to 99.99% — because they don't want to pay credits. And the *actual* observed reliability of S3 over a typical month is even higher, often 99.999%+. Each layer is a buffer: actual reliability > SLO > SLA. This is why AWS publishes the SLA, not the SLO; the SLO is internal engineering truth. **Google** takes this even further: their internal SLO for Search is 99.99% availability, but the SLA for Google Workspace (paid) is 99.9%. The 10× gap between internal target and external promise is intentional buffer.

The SLI is the foundation. A good SLI has two parts: a numerator (good events) and a denominator (all events), both measured the same way over the same window. Examples: "successful HTTP responses / total HTTP responses", "requests served in < 100 ms / total requests", "successful mutations / total mutations". The art is choosing the right SLI — one that captures what users actually experience. A common mistake is choosing an SLI that's easy to measure but doesn't reflect user happiness: measuring "the API returned 200" misses the case where it returned 200 in 30 seconds (user still unhappy). Google's recommendation is to define SLIs around user-visible outcomes: latency for interactive requests, throughput for batch jobs, durability for storage, correctness for data processing.

The SLO is the target. The window matters: a 28-day rolling window is common because it captures both weekday and weekend patterns, is short enough that an incident still hurts the metric, and is long enough that one bad day doesn't blow the entire budget. The classic SLO is "99.9% of requests succeed over 28 days", which translates to an **error budget** of 0.1% × 28 days = 43.2 minutes of allowed unavailability. The error budget is the key SRE innovation: instead of treating reliability as "always 100%", it acknowledges that 100% is impossible and gives engineers a *budget* of allowed unreliability. If you're at 99.95% (under budget), you can ship risky features; if you're at 99.85% (over budget), you freeze features and focus on reliability.

The **error budget** reframes the entire product-engineering relationship. Without it, the conversation is binary: "is the service up?" which leads to either complacency (when it's up) or panic (when it's down). With an error budget, the conversation is quantitative: "you've burned 70% of this month's budget; you have 13 minutes left." This allows product and SRE to negotiate rationally — new feature releases consume budget, and when budget runs low, releases slow down. Google's SRE practice is explicit: if a team is over budget for two consecutive windows, feature releases are frozen until the budget recovers. This is the *SRE hierarchy* in action: monitoring, alerting, error budget, and release freeze, all driven by the SLO.

How SLIs are measured matters. The naïve approach is a Prometheus counter incremented on every request, with a separate counter for "good" requests — `good / total` is your SLI. This works for availability. For latency, you need a histogram (bucketed observations) so you can compute percentiles like p99 — counters can't give you percentiles. **OpenTelemetry** is the modern standard: instrument your code once, export to Prometheus, Datadog, or Honeycomb, and compute SLIs from the resulting metrics. Critical detail: **measure at the right layer**. If you measure SLI at the load balancer, you capture what users see (including LB-induced latency). If you measure at the application, you miss LB failures. Best practice: measure at the LB and join with app-level metrics for the full picture.

Alerting on **burn rate** is how SRE teams operationalize SLOs. Instead of alerting on "current SLO is 99.85%" (which fires too late — by the time the rolling 28-day window dips, you've already burned all the budget), alert on *how fast* the budget is being consumed. A **multi-window multi-burn-rate** alert fires when, say, the 1-hour burn rate is 14.4× the allowed rate *and* the 5-minute burn rate is also 14.4× — meaning you're consuming a full 28-day budget in 2 hours. This catches incidents early without false positives. Google's SRE workbook recommends at least two alerting windows: a fast one (5m / 1h) for acute incidents and a slow one (6h / 24h) for chronic problems. The principle is "alert on symptoms users notice, not on causes engineers notice."

A critical pitfall is **selecting too many SLIs**. A service with 12 SLIs has no SLIs — the team can't prioritize, alerting becomes noisy, and the error budget is meaningless because each SLI has its own budget. Google recommends 1-3 SLIs per user-facing service: typically one for availability (success rate) and one for latency (p99 < threshold). Internal infrastructure services might add a fourth (saturation, freshness). Another pitfall is **gaming the SLI** — if the SLO is "99% of requests return 200", engineers start returning 200 for everything including errors, defeating the metric. The fix is to measure user-perceived outcomes, not protocol-level outcomes: count a response as "good" only if it's both 200 *and* under the latency threshold.

A second pitfall is **calibrating the SLO to current performance rather than to user needs**. If your service currently runs at 99.5% availability and you set the SLO at 99.5%, you've set no target — you've just described the status quo. The SLO should reflect what users *need* (often derived from churn analysis: "users churn if monthly downtime exceeds 30 minutes, so we need 99.9%"). If current performance is below the target, that's the point — the gap is the engineering work. Conversely, if current performance is far above target, you may be over-investing in reliability at the expense of feature velocity; relax the SLO and ship faster.

These concepts connect to the rest of the curriculum. **Availability** (Topic 4) is the most common SLI. **Latency** (Topic 8) percentiles are the second most common. **Throughput** (Topic 9) defines the load level at which the SLI is measured. **Load and stress testing** (Topic 14) validate that the service meets the SLO under expected and beyond-expected traffic. **Horizontal scaling** (Topic 13) is the lever to maintain the SLO as traffic grows. **Reliability** (Topic 5) and **fault tolerance** (Topic 7) determine how often the service breaches the SLO under failure. The error budget is the unifying concept: every other topic either helps you stay within budget (scaling, testing) or consumes budget (incidents, deploys). In practice, the SLI/SLO/SLA hierarchy is the *operating system* of an SRE organization — everything else is implementation.

sections.title: Visual Explanation
sections.body:
### Mermaid Diagram ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Actual reliability
e.g., 99.999%] --> SLO SLO[Internal SLO
e.g., 99.99% over 28d] --> SLA SLA[External SLA
e.g., 99.9% or refund 10%] SLI[SLI: measured ratio
good_events / all_events] -->|compared against| SLO SLO --> EB[Error Budget
0.01% * 28d = 4.3 min] EB --> BU1{Burn rate > 14x?} BU1 -->|Yes, 1h window| Alert1[Page on-call: acute incident] BU1 -->|No| BU2{Burn rate > 3x?} BU2 -->|Yes, 6h window| Alert2[Ticket: chronic problem] BU2 -->|No| OK[Budget healthy: ship features] style A fill:#cfc,stroke:#060 style SLO fill:#eef,stroke:#006 style SLA fill:#fcc,stroke:#600 style EB fill:#ffe,stroke:#660 ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` RELIABILITY HIERARCHY (buffer at every layer) ^ higher reliability (more 9s) | | ACTUAL observed ............ 99.999% (what users actually get) | INTERNAL SLO ................ 99.99% (engineering target) | EXTERNAL SLA ................ 99.9% (contract: refund if missed) | +-----------------------------------------------------> (looser) ERROR BUDGET over 28-day window: SLO 99.9% => budget = 0.1% * 28d * 24h * 60m = 40.3 minutes SLO 99.99% => budget = 0.01% * 28d * 24h * 60m = 4.0 minutes SLO 99.999%=> budget = 0.001% * 28d * 24h * 60m = 0.4 minutes BURN RATE ALERTING (multi-window): +------------------+-------------------+---------------------------+ | Burn rate | Time to exhaust | Action | +------------------+-------------------+---------------------------+ | 1x (steady) | 28 days | Healthy: ship features | | 3x (slow burn) | ~9 days | Ticket: investigate | | 14x (fast burn) | ~2 days | Page on-call | | 60x (acute) | ~11 hours | Page on-call immediately | +------------------+-------------------+---------------------------+ EXAMPLE: AWS S3 ACTUAL ~99.999% > SLO (internal ~99.99%) > SLA (99.9%, 10% credit) ``` ### Walkthrough 1. **Define the SLI.** Pick a user-visible outcome — e.g., "HTTP requests that returned 2xx/3xx in < 200 ms" — and instrument it via OpenTelemetry or Prometheus. The SLI is a ratio: `good_events / total_events` measured over a window. Make sure the measurement is taken at the layer users see (load balancer or client SDK), not at an internal layer that hides failures. 2. **Set the SLO and error budget.** Derive the SLO from user needs (churn analysis, competitive benchmarks), not from current performance. For a 99.9% availability SLO over 28 days, the error budget is 0.1% × 28 × 24 × 60 = 40.3 minutes. Publish the SLO to the team and surface the remaining budget on a dashboard. Make the budget the basis for release decisions: under budget = ship freely; over budget = freeze and remediate. 3. **Alert on burn rate, not on raw SLO.** Configure multi-window alerts: page if 1-hour burn rate > 14× (acute incident) and ticket if 6-hour burn rate > 3× (chronic problem). The 28-day rolling SLO is for reporting, not paging — by the time it dips, you've already failed. The SLA is the legal contract layer; it should always be 10× looser than the SLO so the team has buffer before customer-facing consequences kick in.
